newsitem.title: SUDAN: Former rebels want SPLA head to join Sudan peace.
newsitem.headline: Former rebels want SPLA head to join Sudan peace.

text.p: Southern Sudanese faction leaders who signed a peace deal with Khartoum appealed on Wednesday for main rebel leader John Garang to join them in the agreement, intended to end one of Africa's longest wars.
But Garang was quoted as saying he would continue to fight for the fall of the government, which he said signed the deal on Monday in Khartoum "with itself".
Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) is the mainstream group which has done most of the fighting against the government since war erupted in the south in 1983.

"The war is like a chess game. We made the checkmate move toward the Islamic Front regime," he told al-Hayat newspaper in an interview in the southern town of Yei after the peace deal. "I confirm the Khartoum regime is on its way to falling."
He said SPLA-led rebels aimed to bring about the fall of the government by advancing in the south and east and fomenting an uprising in Khartoum, but they did not want a divided Sudan.
"From day one until now we have called for a new Sudan, not a divided Sudan. We believe in a united Sudan," Garang said.
Khartoum sees the accord as the best hope for ending the war in which the largely Christian and animist south is fighting what it sees as domination by the Moslem and Arab north.

It signed the deal with SPLA-Bahr al-Ghazal, Equatoria Defence Force, Independence of Bor, Southern Sudan Independence Movement (SSIM) and Independence Group of Kawac Makwei, which was named as the South Sudan Independence Group in the accord.
The five factions are united in the agreement under the name United Democratic Salvation Front for Southern Sudan.
"The peace partners welcome John Garang to join the peace march at any moment," Kerubino Kwanyin Bol, head of SPLA Bahr al-Ghazal, said in remarks on the official news agency SUNA.
He said the agreement met all the demands for which southerners were fighting and there was no reason to continue.
The agreement allows southerners to decide in a referendum after a four-year period whether they want unity or secession.
"If war continues, it will not be between the government and Garang's movement but between the south and Garang," said SSIM leader Riek Machar, calling on Garang to join the peace accord.
Equatoria Defence Force leader Thiopholus Ochang Loti called for the deal to ensure peace and stability. Makwei's group said it signalled "the start of rebuilding a new Sudan".
The groups which signed are splinter factions with few forces. Most fought the SPLA as pro-government militias.

Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter discussed with President Omar Hassan al-Bashir last week the possibility of including other groups in the deal. Carter said later Sudan would have to make peace with rebels and neighbours for war to end.
